title: Mock 2 · Futures & Options in Action
blurb: MTM, open interest, portfolio beta, option Greeks and first strategy calculations.

questions.q: The risk that a trader is unable to exit a derivatives position because there are not enough counterparties is called:
questions.explanation: The workbook defines liquidity risk as the inability to exit from a position.
hints: Counterparty risk is the risk of default by the other party.
Correct: inability to exit = liquidity risk.
Operational risk covers fraud, poor documentation and improper execution.
Legal risk concerns enforceability of contracts.

questions.q: Which of the following is a feature of OTC derivative markets, as opposed to exchange-traded derivatives?
options: Prices are discovered through an anonymous auction platform
There are no formal centralised limits on individual positions, leverage or margining
questions.explanation: In OTC markets, contracts are tailor-made, counterparty risk management is decentralised, and there are no formal centralised limits on positions, leverage or margining.
hints: Standardisation is a feature of exchange-traded contracts.
A clearing corporation guarantee is a feature of exchange-traded contracts.
Anonymous auction platforms belong to exchanges.
Correct: OTC markets lack centralised position, leverage and margin limits.

questions.q: The best bid for a stock is ₹100.00 and the best offer is ₹100.50. A large buy order gets executed at an average price of ₹100.75. The impact cost of this buy order is approximately:
hints: This measures from the best offer rather than the ideal (mid) price.
This measures the gap from the best bid instead of the ideal price.
This does not match the formula.

questions.q: A client is long 2 lots of a stock futures contract bought at ₹1,500 today (lot size 250). The daily settlement price is ₹1,488. What is the day's MTM?
questions.explanation: MTM on a new position = (settlement price − trade price) × lot × lots = (1,488 − 1,500) × 250 × 2 = −₹6,000, a debit (MTM loss).
hints: A long position loses when the price falls, so this is a debit, not a credit.
This counts only 1 lot.
This double-counts the loss.

questions.q: A portfolio holds three stocks with weights of 40%, 35% and 25% and betas of 1.2, 0.9 and 1.6 respectively. The portfolio beta is closest to:
hints: This is the simple average of the betas, which ignores the weights.
Correct: weighted average = 1.195 ≈ 1.20.
1.00 is the market beta, not this portfolio's.
Arithmetic error; recompute the weighted sum.

questions.q: Day 1: A buys 100 futures contracts from B (both opening positions). Day 2: A sells 50 contracts to C, who is opening a new long position. What is the open interest at the end of Day 2?
questions.explanation: After Day 1, OI = 100. On Day 2 A closes 50 longs and C opens 50 longs, so A's long is replaced by C's. Longs = A 50 + C 50 = 100 = B's short of 100. OI stays at 100.
hints: OI rises only when both parties open new positions.
OI falls only when both parties close positions.
Correct: one long replaces another, so OI is unchanged at 100.
OI counts only one side of the contracts.

questions.q: Which of the following is an assumption of the cost of carry model of futures pricing?
options: The underlying asset can be sold short
Demand and supply of the underlying are seasonal
questions.explanation: The model assumes abundant supply, non-seasonal demand and supply, easy storage, short selling being possible, and no transaction costs, taxes or margins.
hints: Correct: short selling is assumed to be possible.
The model assumes demand and supply are NOT seasonal.
The model assumes no margin requirements.
The model assumes no transaction costs.

questions.q: Under the expectations model, a market where futures trade below the spot price, indicating an expected fall in the spot price, is called:
questions.explanation: Futures above spot means the market expects prices to rise (contango). Futures below spot means the market expects prices to fall (backwardation).
hints: Contango is futures ABOVE spot.
Convergence describes futures and spot meeting at expiry.
Not a term used in the workbook for this situation.
Correct: futures below spot = backwardation.

questions.q: Nifty is at 24,120. The 24,000-strike put trades at ₹85. What is the time value of this put?
questions.explanation: The put is OTM (S > X), so intrinsic value = max(24,000 − 24,120, 0) = 0. The entire premium of ₹85 is time value.
hints: Correct: the OTM put has zero intrinsic value, so time value = ₹85.
You added the spot-strike gap to the premium.
120 is the amount by which the put is OUT of the money.
You subtracted 120 from 85 wrongly; intrinsic value cannot be negative.

questions.q: You write (sell) a call with a strike of ₹1,000 for a premium of ₹30, lot size 500. At expiry the stock settles at ₹1,070. What is your net P&L?
questions.explanation: Short call payoff = premium − (S − X) = 30 − 70 = −40 per share. For 500 shares: −40 × 500 = −₹20,000.
hints: A short call loses when the price rises above the strike plus premium.
Arithmetic error; recheck the per-share loss of 40.
This ignores the premium received.

questions.q: If the volatility of the underlying rises sharply while other factors stay constant, what happens to option premiums?
options: Call premium rises, put premium falls
Call premium falls, put premium rises
Both call and put premiums rise
questions.explanation: Volatility affects calls and puts in the same way: higher volatility means a greater chance of finishing in the money, so both premiums rise.
hints: That is the effect of a rise in the underlying price (or interest rate).
That is the effect of a fall in the underlying price.
That would be the effect of LOWER volatility.
Correct: higher volatility gives higher premiums for both.

questions.q: A call option has a delta of 0.60. If the underlying stock rises by ₹5, the call premium will change by approximately:
questions.explanation: Change in premium ≈ delta × change in the underlying = 0.60 × 5 = ₹3.00.
hints: That assumes a delta of 1.
Correct: 0.6 × 5 = ₹3.
This is the change for a ₹1 move only.
You divided instead of multiplying.

questions.q: How is implied volatility of an option obtained?
options: As the standard deviation of past weekly returns of the stock
From the beta of the stock
By running an option pricing model such as Black-Scholes in reverse, using the market premium
From the volatility index of another exchange
questions.explanation: Implied volatility is the volatility that makes the model price equal the market premium. It is found by running Black-Scholes in reverse.
hints: That is historical volatility.
Beta measures systematic risk, not volatility of the option.
Correct: IV is backed out of the option premium.
Not the method described in the workbook.

questions.q: A trader sells a 1,200-strike put at ₹40 and buys a 1,150-strike put at ₹15 (same expiry). What is the break-even price of this position?
questions.explanation: This is a bull put spread. Net credit = 40 − 15 = 25. BEP = higher strike − net credit = 1,200 − 25 = ₹1,175.
hints: This subtracts the full 40 premium.
The credit was added instead of subtracted.
This does not follow from the formula.

questions.q: The payoff of a covered call (long stock + short call) resembles which single option position?
questions.explanation: A covered call caps the upside while leaving downside risk, which is the shape of a short put. The workbook calls it a 'synthetic short put'.
hints: A long call is the shape of a protective put.
Correct: a covered call is a synthetic short put.
A long put profits from falls; a covered call loses on falls.
A naked short call loses on rises; a covered call is protected on rises by the stock.

questions.q: Futures prices are rising while open interest is declining. This usually indicates:
questions.explanation: A rising price with falling OI indicates that existing short positions are being squared up, i.e. short covering.
hints: Long build-up = rising price and rising OI.
Short build-up = falling price and rising OI.
Correct: rising price + falling OI = short covering.
Long unwinding = falling price and falling OI.

questions.q: To be eligible for stock derivatives, the stock's median quarter-sigma order size (MQSOS) over the last six months must not be less than:
questions.explanation: Eligibility requires MQSOS of at least ₹75 lakh, MWPL of at least ₹1,500 crore, average daily delivery value of at least ₹35 crore, and a place in the top 500 stocks.
hints: Too low.
Too low.
Too high.
Correct: ₹75 lakh.

questions.q: A trader holding shares bought at ₹500 places a stop-loss sell order with a trigger price of ₹480 and a limit price of ₹475. When does this order become an active limit sell order?
options: When the market price falls to or below the trigger of ₹480
Only at the end of the trading day
questions.explanation: A stop-loss order is activated when the trigger price is reached or crossed. It then enters the market as a limit order at ₹475.
hints: ₹475 is the limit price, not the trigger.
Correct: the order activates at the ₹480 trigger.
It sits in the stop-loss book until triggered.
It activates whenever the trigger is hit during the day.

questions.q: For F&O adjustment purposes, a dividend is treated as 'extraordinary' (requiring strike adjustment) when it exceeds what percentage of the market value of the underlying stock?
questions.explanation: Dividends below 2% of market value are ordinary and need no adjustment. Above 2% they are extraordinary, and the strike prices are reduced by the dividend.
hints: Wrong threshold.
Wrong threshold.
Wrong threshold.
Correct: 2%.

questions.q: Initial margin requirements in the equity derivatives segment are based on which Value-at-Risk measure?
questions.explanation: Initial margin is based on 99% VaR over one day. For futures, where MTM may not be collected before the next day opens, a two-day horizon is applied.
hints: Correct: 99%, one day.
The confidence level is too low.
The horizon is too long.
The confidence level is wrong; two days applies to futures only, and at 99%.

questions.q: A client holds one lot (75) of an index call with a strike of 24,000. The index settles at 24,180 on expiry. What is the final settlement amount the client receives?
questions.explanation: Index options are cash-settled at intrinsic value: (24,180 − 24,000) × 75 = 180 × 75 = ₹13,500, credited on T+1.
hints: That is the notional at strike; index options are not physically settled.
A decimal place is wrong.
This adds notional and payoff.

questions.q: Delivery margins on physically settled derivatives are collected in a staggered manner. What percentage is levied at the end of day on Expiry − 2?
questions.explanation: Staggering: 20% at E−4, 40% at E−3, 60% at E−2 and 80% at E−1 EOD.
hints: 20% applies at E−4.
40% applies at E−3.
Correct: 60% at E−2.
80% applies at E−1.

questions.q: As per the L.C. Gupta committee norms, a derivatives exchange or segment should have a minimum of how many members?
questions.explanation: The exchange should have a minimum of 50 members. Trading and clearing members may make up at most 40% of the governing council.
hints: 40% is the cap on broker representation on the governing council.
Too high.
Too low.
Correct: 50 members.

questions.q: Unabsorbed losses from derivatives transactions on a recognised stock exchange can be carried forward for how many assessment years?
questions.explanation: Such losses can be carried forward for 8 assessment years and set off against non-speculative business income, provided the return is filed by the due date.
hints: Correct: 8 assessment years.
Wrong period.
Wrong period.
Wrong period.

questions.q: In the KYC/AML framework, Politically Exposed Persons (PEPs) are classified as:
questions.explanation: PEPs are listed among Clients of Special Category (CSC), along with NRIs, HNIs, trusts and others, and require enhanced due diligence.
hints: PEPs are not institutions.
PEPs are higher risk, not low risk.
Correct: Clients of Special Category.
This classification ignores their special risk.
